verses.1: O LORD, blessed be my rock, the one who taught my hands for battle, my fingers for war.
verses.2: My steadfast love and my refuge, my defender and my deliverer, my shield in whom I have trusted. You have placed my people under my care.
verses.3: O LORD, what is a human that you know him, or a son of man that you consider him?
verses.4: A human is like a fleeting breath; his days are like a passing shadow.
verses.5: O LORD, bend your heavens and come down, touch the mountains and let them burn.
verses.6: Flash lightning and scatter them; send out your arrows and disorient them.
verses.7: Send your hand from on high, rescue me, and deliver me from many waters, from the hands of foreigners.
verses.8: Those whose mouths speak falsehood, and whose right hands are hands of deceit.
verses.9: O God, I will sing to you a new song; with a ten-stringed lyre I will praise you.
verses.10: The one who gives salvation to kings, who delivers your servant David from the evil sword.
verses.11: Rescue me and deliver me from the hands of foreigners, whose mouths speak falsehood, and whose right hands are hands of deceit.
verses.12: Those whose children are like well-planted vines, growing in their youth; their daughters like well-woven tapestries, adorned like the design of a temple.
verses.13: Their storehouses are full, producing grain from one to another; their flocks multiply, bearing abundantly in their fields.
verses.14: Their cattle are strong; there is no broken fence, no going out, no cry in their villages.
verses.15: Happy is the people who are like this, happy is the people whose God is the LORD.

notes:
Notes
- v. 1: "the one who taught my hands for battle" reflects the poetic parallelism and the military imagery of the psalm.
- v. 11: Repetition of v. 7 is likely intentional for emphasis and poetic structure.
- v. 12–14: These verses present a vision of peace and prosperity, rendered in concrete, agricultural imagery. The metaphor of "well-woven tapestries" is used to capture the Hebrew phrase "kethav yakhud" (literally "woven together").
raw:
[1] O LORD, blessed be my rock, the one who taught my hands for battle, my fingers for war.

[2] My steadfast love and my refuge, my defender and my deliverer, my shield in whom I have trusted. You have placed my people under my care.

[3] O LORD, what is a human that you know him, or a son of man that you consider him?

[4] A human is like a fleeting breath; his days are like a passing shadow.

[5] O LORD, bend your heavens and come down, touch the mountains and let them burn.

[6] Flash lightning and scatter them; send out your arrows and disorient them.

[7] Send your hand from on high, rescue me, and deliver me from many waters, from the hands of foreigners.

[8] Those whose mouths speak falsehood, and whose right hands are hands of deceit.

[9] O God, I will sing to you a new song; with a ten-stringed lyre I will praise you.

[10] The one who gives salvation to kings, who delivers your servant David from the evil sword.

[11] Rescue me and deliver me from the hands of foreigners, whose mouths speak falsehood, and whose right hands are hands of deceit.

[12] Those whose children are like well-planted vines, growing in their youth; their daughters like well-woven tapestries, adorned like the design of a temple.

[13] Their storehouses are full, producing grain from one to another; their flocks multiply, bearing abundantly in their fields.

[14] Their cattle are strong; there is no broken fence, no going out, no cry in their villages.

[15] Happy is the people who are like this, happy is the people whose God is the LORD.

---
Notes
- v. 1: "the one who taught my hands for battle" reflects the poetic parallelism and the military imagery of the psalm.
- v. 11: Repetition of v. 7 is likely intentional for emphasis and poetic structure.
- v. 12–14: These verses present a vision of peace and prosperity, rendered in concrete, agricultural imagery. The metaphor of "well-woven tapestries" is used to capture the Hebrew phrase "kethav yakhud" (literally "woven together").
